title: Do Teachers Dream of GenAI Widening Educational (In)equality? Envisioning the Future of K-12 GenAI Education from Global Teachers’ Perspectives
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers think about and teach generative AI (GenAI) in relation to educational equality. The central question is how teachers are already integrating GenAI into classroom practice, what structural barriers constrain those efforts, and what kinds of support they believe are needed to make GenAI education more equitable.

The study is based on 30 semi-structured interviews with K–12 teachers in the United States, South Africa, and Taiwan. Participants taught across elementary, middle, and high school settings, with subject areas including English, social science, math, science, special education, information technology, and computer science. Some teachers taught formal AI/IT courses, while others incorporated GenAI into ordinary subject teaching. The paper is therefore not an intervention study but an exploratory qualitative study of teachers’ current practices and future visions in diverse school contexts.

The main findings are that teachers see GenAI as both an opportunity and a risk for educational inequality. They described using GenAI to help students in under-resourced settings, support learners with limited digital literacy, and provide personalized assistance for marginalized students. At the same time, they worried that GenAI could intensify inequality through shortcut learning, bullying, cultural bias, and overreliance that replaces human care. Teachers also reported systemic barriers such as unequal infrastructure, limited professional training, and restrictive norms, and they called for support from schools, policymakers, and technology companies. The paper concludes that equitable GenAI education depends on broader sociotechnical support, not only individual teacher effort.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools/chatbots used for generating and interacting with text, explanations, and other content; no specific commercial or research product is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: K–12 teachers were interviewed about how they teach students about generative AI, including using it in lessons, assignments, and classroom discussions across subjects and settings.

findings.finding_summary: This qualitative interview study with 30 K–12 teachers across the United States, South Africa, and Taiwan found that teachers viewed GenAI as both a tool for reducing pre-existing educational inequalities and a source of new risks. Teachers described using GenAI to address resource shortages, support digital literacy, and personalize learning, while also reporting structural barriers such as unequal infrastructure, insufficient training, and restrictive norms.
findings.measure: Teacher interview accounts of GenAI integration, constraints, and perceived equality implications

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, cross-national interview study rather than an experimental evaluation. It provides rich descriptive evidence about teacher experiences and contexts, but no causal effect estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports important systemic and practice-level implications, but it does not measure outcome gains or provide effect sizes. Impact is therefore important but empirically unquantified.
